§3.3 Boxes and Granularity

📄 Page rule — applied from the page alone

output-boxes-and-granularity · output output-model boxes layout

✅ Normative

A box is the region of the page that an element's printed content occupies. Boxes MUST be given at exactly the granularity that was requested, and at that granularity every element MUST have one box. A producer MUST NOT return several granularities in place of one.

What a box covers

A box MUST enclose all of its element's printed content and SHOULD enclose nothing else. What belongs to an element — whether a caption is inside a table's box, whether a list item's box includes its bullet, where a picture ends — is decided by the layout rules: Block Boundaries§5.2, Block Annotation§5.1 and Block Classes§5.3. A box never covers content moved out of its position in the Markdown: a watermark's box is where the watermark is printed.

The four levels

Level A box is given for… Suited to
none each element (region level) the default: region-level grounding
cell each element, and each table cell per-value verification and highlighting
line each element, and each printed line line-level citation, reading-order checks
word each element, and each word per-token grounding

The levels are a ladder

The levels subsume one another, and the resolution rule is strict precedence:

word  >  line  >  cell  >  none

A request naming several levels MUST be served at the finest one named; naming coarser levels alongside it changes nothing.

Choosing a level

Finer is not better. Each step down multiplies the number of boxes, and every box can be wrong, mis-attributed or drift out of alignment with its text. A consumer SHOULD request the coarsest level that answers its question.

Where a rule turns on geometry — is this value printed once or three times? does this ruling line stop before that column? — the evidence lives at cell level or finer. A coarser output can neither settle nor dispute those questions.
